name: Accuracy
description: Fraction of observations whose predicted label equals the true label.
limitations: Misleading under class imbalance: a constant majority-class predictor can score highly.

name: Precision
description: Of the observations predicted positive, the fraction that are truly positive.
assumptions: Multiclass and multilabel inputs require an explicit `average` (micro, macro, weighted, samples, or None).
limitations: Undefined when there are no positive predictions; handled by `zero_division`.

name: Recall
description: Of the truly positive observations, the fraction predicted positive. Equal to sensitivity in the binary case.
assumptions: Multiclass and multilabel inputs require an explicit `average` (micro, macro, weighted, samples, or None).
limitations: Undefined when a class has no true instances; handled by `zero_division`.

name: F1 score
description: Harmonic mean of precision and recall.
formula: F1 = 2 · Precision · Recall / (Precision + Recall) = 2TP / (2TP + FP + FN)
assumptions: Multiclass and multilabel inputs require an explicit `average` (micro, macro, weighted, samples, or None).
limitations: Ignores true negatives.
Macro, micro, and weighted averages can rank models differently.

references.citation: van Rijsbergen, C. J. (1979). Information Retrieval (2nd ed.). Butterworths.

name: Balanced accuracy
description: Mean of per-class recall. Reduces the influence of class imbalance compared with accuracy.

references.citation: Brodersen, K. H., Ong, C. S., Stephan, K. E., & Buhmann, J. M. (2010). The balanced accuracy and its posterior distribution. Proceedings of the 20th International Conference on Pattern Recognition, 3121–3124.

name: Matthews correlation coefficient
description: Correlation between observed and predicted binary labels that uses all four confusion-matrix cells.
limitations: Undefined when any marginal of the confusion matrix is zero; EvalSuite reports this explicitly rather than returning a silent value.

references.citation: Matthews, B. W. (1975). Comparison of the predicted and observed secondary structure of T4 phage lysozyme. Biochimica et Biophysica Acta, 405(2), 442–451.

name: Cohen's kappa
description: Agreement between predicted and true labels corrected for agreement expected by chance.
limitations: Depends on the marginal distributions, so values are hard to compare across datasets with different prevalence.

references.citation: Cohen, J. (1960). A coefficient of agreement for nominal scales. Educational and Psychological Measurement, 20(1), 37–46.

name: ROC AUC
description: Area under the receiver operating characteristic curve; the probability that a random positive is ranked above a random negative.
inputs: y_prob: predicted probability of the positive class in [0, 1]
assumptions: Requires both classes to be present in y_true.
limitations: Insensitive to calibration.
Can look optimistic on heavily imbalanced data; consider PR AUC alongside it.

references.citation: Hanley, J. A., & McNeil, B. J. (1982). The meaning and use of the area under a receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve. Radiology, 143(1), 29–36.
Fawcett, T. (2006). An introduction to ROC analysis. Pattern Recognition Letters, 27(8), 861–874.

name: PR AUC (average precision)
description: Summary of the precision-recall curve, computed as average precision over recall steps.
inputs: y_prob: predicted probability of the positive class in [0, 1]
limitations: The baseline equals prevalence, so values are not comparable across datasets with different prevalence.
Trapezoidal interpolation of PR curves is optimistic; average precision avoids it.

references.citation: Davis, J., & Goadrich, M. (2006). The relationship between precision-recall and ROC curves. Proceedings of the 23rd International Conference on Machine Learning, 233–240.
Saito, T., & Rehmsmeier, M. (2015). The precision-recall plot is more informative than the ROC plot when evaluating binary classifiers on imbalanced datasets. PLOS ONE, 10(3), e0118432.

name: Log loss
description: Negative mean log-likelihood of the true labels under the predicted probabilities.
formula: LogLoss = −(1/N) Σᵢ [yᵢ log pᵢ + (1 − yᵢ) log(1 − pᵢ)]
inputs: y_prob: predicted probability of the positive class in [0, 1]
limitations: Unbounded for confident wrong predictions; probabilities are clipped and the clipping value is reported.

name: Confusion matrix
description: Counts of true versus predicted labels. Computed once per evaluation and shared by every count-based metric.
formula: Cᵢⱼ = #{n : yₙ = i and ŷₙ = j}

name: Mean absolute error
description: Average absolute difference between predictions and targets, in target units.

references.citation: Willmott, C. J., & Matsuura, K. (2005). Advantages of the mean absolute error (MAE) over the root mean square error (RMSE) in assessing average model performance. Climate Research, 30(1), 79–82.

name: Mean squared error
description: Average squared difference between predictions and targets.
limitations: Sensitive to outliers because errors are squared.

name: Root mean squared error
description: Square root of MSE, expressed in target units.
limitations: Sensitive to outliers.

references.citation: Willmott, C. J., & Matsuura, K. (2005). Advantages of the mean absolute error (MAE) over the root mean square error (RMSE) in assessing average model performance. Climate Research, 30(1), 79–82.

name: Coefficient of determination (R²)
description: Proportion of variance in the target explained by the predictions, relative to predicting the mean.
limitations: Undefined for constant targets; reported explicitly rather than returned as a number.

name: Adjusted R²
description: R² penalised for the number of predictors in the model.

name: Mean absolute percentage error
description: Average absolute error relative to the magnitude of the target.
assumptions: All targets must be non-zero; zero targets raise a validation error.
limitations: Asymmetric: penalises over-prediction and under-prediction differently.

references.citation: Hyndman, R. J., & Koehler, A. B. (2006). Another look at measures of forecast accuracy. International Journal of Forecasting, 22(4), 679–688.

name: Symmetric MAPE
description: Percentage error scaled by the mean magnitude of target and prediction.
limitations: Several conflicting definitions exist; EvalSuite documents the one it uses.

references.citation: Hyndman, R. J., & Koehler, A. B. (2006). Another look at measures of forecast accuracy. International Journal of Forecasting, 22(4), 679–688.

name: Root mean squared log error
description: RMSE computed on log(1 + value), emphasising relative rather than absolute error.
assumptions: Targets and predictions must be greater than −1; invalid domains raise a validation error.

name: Median absolute error
description: Median of absolute errors; robust to outliers.

name: Huber loss
description: Quadratic for small errors and linear for large errors, controlled by δ.
formula: Lδ(e) = ½e² if |e| ≤ δ, else δ(|e| − ½δ)

references.citation: Huber, P. J. (1964). Robust estimation of a location parameter. The Annals of Mathematical Statistics, 35(1), 73–101.

name: Quantile (pinball) loss
description: Asymmetric loss used to evaluate quantile predictions.

references.citation: Koenker, R., & Bassett, G. (1978). Regression quantiles. Econometrica, 46(1), 33–50.

name: Sensitivity
description: Proportion of people with the condition whom the test correctly identifies as positive.
assumptions: Binary reference standard is treated as ground truth.

references.citation: Altman, D. G., & Bland, J. M. (1994). Diagnostic tests 1: sensitivity and specificity. BMJ, 308(6943), 1552.

name: Specificity
description: Proportion of people without the condition whom the test correctly identifies as negative.

references.citation: Altman, D. G., & Bland, J. M. (1994). Diagnostic tests 1: sensitivity and specificity. BMJ, 308(6943), 1552.

name: Positive predictive value
description: Probability that a person with a positive result has the condition.
limitations: Depends on prevalence; values from one population do not transfer to another with different prevalence.

references.citation: Altman, D. G., & Bland, J. M. (1994). Diagnostic tests 2: predictive values. BMJ, 309(6947), 102.

name: Negative predictive value
description: Probability that a person with a negative result does not have the condition.
limitations: Depends on prevalence.

references.citation: Altman, D. G., & Bland, J. M. (1994). Diagnostic tests 2: predictive values. BMJ, 309(6947), 102.

name: Positive likelihood ratio
description: How much a positive result increases the odds of the condition.
limitations: Infinite when specificity is 1; reported explicitly.

name: Negative likelihood ratio
description: How much a negative result decreases the odds of the condition.

name: Diagnostic odds ratio
description: Ratio of the odds of a positive result in people with the condition to the odds in people without it.
limitations: Undefined when FP or FN is zero unless a continuity correction is requested explicitly.

references.citation: Glas, A. S., Lijmer, J. G., Prins, M. H., Bonsel, G. J., & Bossuyt, P. M. M. (2003). The diagnostic odds ratio: a single indicator of test performance. Journal of Clinical Epidemiology, 56(11), 1129–1135.

example:
es.diagnostic_odds_ratio(y_true, y_pred)
es.diagnostic_report(y_true, y_pred)  # every measure with a CI

name: Youden's J
description: Single summary of sensitivity and specificity at one threshold.
limitations: Weights false positives and false negatives equally, which rarely matches clinical costs.

references.citation: Youden, W. J. (1950). Index for rating diagnostic tests. Cancer, 3(1), 32–35.

name: Net benefit (decision curve analysis)
description: Clinical utility of a model across threshold probabilities, compared with treat-all and treat-none strategies.
inputs: y_prob: predicted probability of the positive class in [0, 1]
assumptions: Threshold probability reflects the relative harm of false positives and false negatives.
limitations: Net benefit is relative to the evaluation population and its prevalence.

references.citation: Vickers, A. J., & Elkin, E. B. (2006). Decision curve analysis: a novel method for evaluating prediction models. Medical Decision Making, 26(6), 565–574.

name: Brier score
description: Mean squared difference between predicted probabilities and binary outcomes.
inputs: y_prob: predicted probability of the positive class in [0, 1]
limitations: Mixes calibration and discrimination; a low score alone does not show good calibration.

references.citation: Brier, G. W. (1950). Verification of forecasts expressed in terms of probability. Monthly Weather Review, 78(1), 1–3.

name: Expected calibration error
description: Weighted average gap between predicted confidence and observed frequency across probability bins.
inputs: y_prob: predicted probability of the positive class in [0, 1]
limitations: Depends on the number of bins and the binning strategy, which are always reported with the value.

references.citation: Naeini, M. P., Cooper, G. F., & Hauskrecht, M. (2015). Obtaining well calibrated probabilities using Bayesian binning. Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence, 29(1).

name: Maximum calibration error
description: Largest gap between confidence and observed frequency over all bins.
inputs: y_prob: predicted probability of the positive class in [0, 1]
limitations: Dominated by sparsely populated bins.

references.citation: Naeini, M. P., Cooper, G. F., & Hauskrecht, M. (2015). Obtaining well calibrated probabilities using Bayesian binning. Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence, 29(1).

name: Calibration slope and intercept
description: Coefficients of a logistic regression of the outcome on the logit of the predicted probability.
formula: logit P(y = 1) = a + b · logit(p);  ideal a = 0, b = 1
inputs: y_prob: predicted probability of the positive class in [0, 1]
limitations: Summarises calibration with two numbers; inspect the calibration curve as well.

references.citation: Cox, D. R. (1958). Two further applications of a model for binary regression. Biometrika, 45(3/4), 562–565.

name: Hosmer–Lemeshow test
description: Goodness-of-fit test comparing observed and expected event counts across risk groups.
formula: H = Σ_g (O_g − E_g)² / (E_g (1 − E_g / n_g)),  df = G − 2
inputs: y_prob: predicted probability of the positive class in [0, 1]
limitations: Results depend on the grouping.
Low power in small samples and near-certain rejection in very large samples.
A non-significant result does not show that calibration is good.

references.citation: Hosmer, D. W., & Lemeshow, S. (1980). Goodness of fit tests for the multiple logistic regression model. Communications in Statistics – Theory and Methods, 9(10), 1035–1049.

name: Wilson score interval
description: Confidence interval for a binomial proportion with good coverage for small samples and extreme proportions.

references.citation: Wilson, E. B. (1927). Probable inference, the law of succession, and statistical inference. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 22(158), 209–212.

name: Clopper–Pearson interval
description: Exact binomial interval obtained by inverting two one-sided binomial tests.
formula: Lower = B(α/2; k, n − k + 1),  Upper = B(1 − α/2; k + 1, n − k)
limitations: Conservative: coverage is at least the nominal level, so intervals are wider than necessary.

references.citation: Clopper, C. J., & Pearson, E. S. (1934). The use of confidence or fiducial limits illustrated in the case of the binomial. Biometrika, 26(4), 404–413.

name: Percentile bootstrap
description: Interval from the empirical quantiles of a statistic recomputed on resampled data.
limitations: Can under-cover for skewed or biased statistics; BCa corrects for bias and skewness.

references.citation: Efron, B. (1979). Bootstrap methods: another look at the jackknife. The Annals of Statistics, 7(1), 1–26.

name: BCa bootstrap
description: Bias-corrected and accelerated bootstrap interval.
formula: Percentiles adjusted by bias correction z₀ and acceleration a (jackknife)
limitations: Requires a jackknife pass, which adds N extra evaluations of the statistic.

references.citation: Efron, B. (1987). Better bootstrap confidence intervals. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 82(397), 171–185.

name: Independent-samples t-test
description: Tests whether two independent groups have equal means. Welch's version does not assume equal variances.
assumptions: Approximately normal sampling distribution of the mean.

references.citation: Student. (1908). The probable error of a mean. Biometrika, 6(1), 1–25.
Welch, B. L. (1947). The generalization of 'Student's' problem when several different population variances are involved. Biometrika, 34(1–2), 28–35.

example: es.t_test(scores_a, scores_b)  # Welch; equal_var=True for Student

name: Paired t-test
description: Tests whether the mean of paired differences is zero, for example per-fold scores of two models.
limitations: Cross-validation folds are not independent; the test can be anti-conservative for model comparison.

references.citation: Student. (1908). The probable error of a mean. Biometrika, 6(1), 1–25.

name: Mann–Whitney U test
description: Rank-based test for whether one of two independent samples tends to have larger values.

references.citation: Mann, H. B., & Whitney, D. R. (1947). On a test of whether one of two random variables is stochastically larger than the other. The Annals of Mathematical Statistics, 18(1), 50–60.

name: Wilcoxon signed-rank test
description: Rank-based test for paired samples.
formula: W = Σ rank(|dᵢ|) over positive dᵢ
assumptions: Differences are symmetric about the median.

references.citation: Wilcoxon, F. (1945). Individual comparisons by ranking methods. Biometrics Bulletin, 1(6), 80–83.

name: Kruskal–Wallis test
description: Rank-based test comparing three or more independent groups.

references.citation: Kruskal, W. H., & Wallis, W. A. (1952). Use of ranks in one-criterion variance analysis. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 47(260), 583–621.

name: Friedman test
description: Rank-based test for three or more related samples, such as several models evaluated on the same datasets.

references.citation: Friedman, M. (1937). The use of ranks to avoid the assumption of normality implicit in the analysis of variance. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 32(200), 675–701.

name: McNemar's test
description: Compares two classifiers on the same observations using their discordant predictions.
limitations: Use the exact binomial version when b + c is small.

references.citation: McNemar, Q. (1947). Note on the sampling error of the difference between correlated proportions or percentages. Psychometrika, 12(2), 153–157.

name: Shapiro–Wilk test
description: Tests the null hypothesis that a sample comes from a normal distribution.
limitations: With large samples, trivial departures from normality become significant.

references.citation: Shapiro, S. S., & Wilk, M. B. (1965). An analysis of variance test for normality (complete samples). Biometrika, 52(3–4), 591–611.

name: DeLong test for correlated ROC AUCs
description: Compares the ROC AUCs of two models evaluated on the same observations.
formula: z = (AUC₁ − AUC₂) / √Var(AUC₁ − AUC₂), variance from structural components

references.citation: DeLong, E. R., DeLong, D. M., & Clarke-Pearson, D. L. (1988). Comparing the areas under two or more correlated receiver operating characteristic curves: a nonparametric approach. Biometrics, 44(3), 837–845.

name: Cohen's d
description: Standardised mean difference using the pooled standard deviation.
limitations: Conventional small/medium/large thresholds are context-free rules of thumb.

references.citation: Cohen, J. (1988). Statistical Power Analysis for the Behavioral Sciences (2nd ed.). Lawrence Erlbaum Associates.

name: Hedges' g
description: Cohen's d with a small-sample bias correction.

references.citation: Hedges, L. V. (1981). Distribution theory for Glass's estimator of effect size and related estimators. Journal of Educational Statistics, 6(2), 107–128.

name: Cramér's V
description: Strength of association between two categorical variables.

references.citation: Cramér, H. (1946). Mathematical Methods of Statistics. Princeton University Press.

name: Bonferroni correction
description: Controls the family-wise error rate by multiplying each p-value by the number of tests.
limitations: Conservative when tests are positively correlated.

references.citation: Dunn, O. J. (1961). Multiple comparisons among means. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 56(293), 52–64.

name: Holm step-down
description: Sequentially rejective procedure that controls the family-wise error rate and is uniformly more powerful than Bonferroni.

references.citation: Holm, S. (1979). A simple sequentially rejective multiple test procedure. Scandinavian Journal of Statistics, 6(2), 65–70.

name: Hochberg step-up
description: Step-up procedure controlling the family-wise error rate under independence or certain positive dependence.
formula: Reject H₍₁₎…H₍ₖ₎ for the largest k with p₍ₖ₎ ≤ α / (m − k + 1)

references.citation: Hochberg, Y. (1988). A sharper Bonferroni procedure for multiple tests of significance. Biometrika, 75(4), 800–802.

name: Benjamini–Hochberg (FDR)
description: Controls the expected proportion of false discoveries among rejected hypotheses.
formula: Reject H₍₁₎…H₍ₖ₎ for the largest k with p₍ₖ₎ ≤ (k / m) α
assumptions: Independent or positively dependent test statistics.

references.citation: Benjamini, Y., & Hochberg, Y. (1995). Controlling the false discovery rate: a practical and powerful approach to multiple testing. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series B, 57(1), 289–300.

name: Dice coefficient
description: Overlap between predicted and ground-truth masks, weighting the intersection twice.
inputs: y_pred: predicted mask with the same shape
limitations: Undefined when both masks are empty; the `empty` policy (1.0, NaN, or exclude) is always explicit.

references.citation: Dice, L. R. (1945). Measures of the amount of ecologic association between species. Ecology, 26(3), 297–302.

name: Intersection over union
description: Ratio of the intersection to the union of predicted and ground-truth masks (Jaccard index).
inputs: y_pred: predicted mask with the same shape

references.citation: Jaccard, P. (1912). The distribution of the flora in the alpine zone. New Phytologist, 11(2), 37–50.

name: Mean IoU
description: IoU averaged over classes, with support for ignore_index.
inputs: y_pred: predicted mask with the same shape

references.citation: Long, J., Shelhamer, E., & Darrell, T. (2015). Fully convolutional networks for semantic segmentation. Proceedings of the IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition, 3431–3440.

name: Pixel accuracy
description: Fraction of correctly labelled pixels.
inputs: y_pred: predicted mask with the same shape
limitations: Dominated by large classes such as background.

references.citation: Long, J., Shelhamer, E., & Darrell, T. (2015). Fully convolutional networks for semantic segmentation. Proceedings of the IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition, 3431–3440.

name: Boundary IoU
description: IoU computed on contour bands of fixed width, emphasising boundary quality.
formula: Boundary IoU = |(G_d ∩ G) ∩ (P_d ∩ P)| / |(G_d ∩ G) ∪ (P_d ∩ P)|
inputs: y_pred: predicted mask with the same shape

references.citation: Cheng, B., Girshick, R., Dollár, P., Berg, A. C., & Kirillov, A. (2021). Boundary IoU: Improving object-centric image segmentation evaluation. Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition, 15334–15342.

name: Hausdorff distance
description: Largest distance from a point on one boundary to the nearest point on the other.
formula: H(A, B) = max(supₐ inf_b d(a, b), sup_b infₐ d(a, b))
inputs: y_pred: predicted mask with the same shape
limitations: Sensitive to single outlier pixels; a percentile variant (HD95) is planned.

references.citation: Huttenlocher, D. P., Klanderman, G. A., & Rucklidge, W. J. (1993). Comparing images using the Hausdorff distance. IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence, 15(9), 850–863.

name: Box IoU
description: Intersection over union of two axis-aligned bounding boxes.
assumptions: Boxes must satisfy x2 ≥ x1 and y2 ≥ y1; invalid boxes raise a validation error.

name: Average precision
description: Area under the interpolated precision-recall curve for one class at one IoU threshold.
inputs: ground truth: boxes [x1, y1, x2, y2] with class labels
predictions: boxes with class labels and confidence scores
limitations: Interpolation and matching conventions differ between VOC and COCO; the convention used is documented with every result.

references.citation: Everingham, M., Van Gool, L., Williams, C. K. I., Winn, J., & Zisserman, A. (2010). The PASCAL Visual Object Classes (VOC) challenge. International Journal of Computer Vision, 88(2), 303–338.

name: mAP@[.50:.95]
description: Mean AP over classes and over IoU thresholds 0.50, 0.55, …, 0.95.
inputs: ground truth: boxes [x1, y1, x2, y2] with class labels
predictions: boxes with class labels and confidence scores
limitations: Not claimed to be COCO-compatible unless verified against the reference COCO evaluation protocol.

references.citation: Lin, T.-Y., Maire, M., Belongie, S., Hays, J., Perona, P., Ramanan, D., Dollár, P., & Zitnick, C. L. (2014). Microsoft COCO: Common objects in context. European Conference on Computer Vision (ECCV), 740–755.
